book.title: The Power of a Positive No
book.subtitle: How to Say No and Still Get to Yes
book.author_credibility: Ury cofounded Harvard's Program on Negotiation, coauthored Getting to Yes, and has worked as a mediator in labor and international conflicts. The book is based on a course he taught at Harvard for managers and professionals. As a practitioner and trainer he has an interest in the method's popularity.
book.evidence_base: Practitioner synthesis from negotiation and mediation experience, illustrated with stories (corporate, political, and family). Consistent with interest-based negotiation principles, but the three-step method itself has not been empirically tested.

legal_access.note: Publisher reader's guide with chapter-linked discussion questions and Ury's Yes! No. Yes? rehearsal exercise.

insights.name: Yes! No. Yes?: The Positive No
insights.explanation: Ury's alternative to a bare refusal is a no that starts and ends with a yes. First, a Yes to what you are protecting: the interest, need, or value that makes the no necessary (your team's capacity, time with your family, a quality standard). Second, a plain No to the specific request or behavior, stated as a matter of fact without an edge, apology, or lecture. Third, a Yes? that proposes something the other person can accept: a concrete alternative, a different time, a referral, or simply an affirmation of the relationship. The shape is 'Because I need X, I am not able to do Y; what I can do is Z.' Grounding the no in your own yes makes it steadier and less personal, and the closing proposal gives the other person somewhere to go. Ury suggests rehearsing the three parts aloud and asking listeners whether it sounded too accommodating, too attacking, or too avoidant.
insights.when_to_use: When you need to refuse a request, demand, or behavior from someone whose relationship you want to keep: a boss, a client, a colleague, a partner, a parent, a child.
insights.worked_example: A manager asks a senior analyst to lead a new reporting project. She replies: 'I want the Q3 audit to land on time and done well, because the board is relying on it (Yes!). So I am not going to take on the reporting project this quarter (No). I can scope it with you now so it is ready to start in October, or suggest Priya, who has asked for a lead role (Yes?).' At home, when his mother proposes staying for two weeks over the holidays, a man says: 'We really want the kids to have time with you, and we also need the house to stay calm for Maya's recovery. Two weeks is more than we can manage this year. Could you come for the long weekend, and we will all go to the lake house in the spring?'
common_mistakes: Leading with the no, so the other person hears rejection before they hear why
Burying the no in so much apology or explanation that it sounds like a maybe
Making the closing yes vague ('let me know if there is anything else') instead of a specific proposal
Using the first yes to praise the other person rather than to name what you are protecting
Adding judgment ('you always do this') that turns a no into an attack
steps: Before the conversation, identify your underlying Yes: the interest, need, or value at stake
Write the No as one plain sentence about the request or behavior, not about the person
Prepare a specific, realistic Yes? proposal the other person could accept
Deliver all three in order, calmly and briefly
Rehearse with someone and ask whether it sounded accommodating, attacking, avoidant, or right
situations: Declining a new project from your manager
Turning down a request to review someone's work

source.citation: William Ury, The Power of a Positive No (2007), introduction and Part II on delivering a Positive No; publisher reader's guide, 'Delivering a Positive No' exercise
source.underlying_research: None tested; draws on interest-based negotiation (Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes).

insights.confidence_rationale: Credible expert practice from a leading negotiation scholar and mediator, confirmed in the publisher's own reader's guide exercise. The method is untested as a package; research on refusals (for example Givi and Kirk, 2024) supports that a considerate no carries less cost than people fear, but does not test this specific structure.

insights.name: The Three-A Trap: Accommodate, Attack, Avoid
insights.explanation: When someone asks for something we do not want to give, Ury says we usually fall into one of three traps. Accommodating means saying yes when we mean no, valuing the relationship over our own interests. Attacking means saying no badly, with anger or contempt, valuing our interests over the relationship. Avoiding means saying nothing and hoping the problem goes away. The traps often chain together: we dodge a request, it comes back again, we snap, feel guilty, and then give in. Knowing which trap you default to, and with whom, tells you what to practice. The Positive No is meant to escape all three by protecting both the interest and the relationship.
insights.when_to_use: When you notice repeated resentment, guilt, or blow-ups around requests from a particular person, or when preparing for a refusal you have been putting off.
insights.worked_example: An operations manager realizes that with one demanding vice president she always accommodates, staying late on last-minute requests, while with her own team she tends to avoid saying no and then snaps when work piles up. Naming the pattern helps: with the VP she practices stating a limit and an alternative, and with her team she commits to answering requests within a day rather than letting them hang. A college student sees the same chain with a roommate who borrows things: he ignored it for weeks, exploded over a missing jacket, felt bad, and then offered his car.
common_mistakes: Assuming you only have one style, when people often accommodate with some people and attack with others
Swinging from accommodation straight to attack once resentment builds
Overcorrecting into rigid refusals after realizing you accommodate too much
steps: Recall your last few difficult requests and label your response: accommodate, attack, or avoid
Notice whether the pattern changes with who is asking
Watch for the chain: avoidance, repeated asks, a sharp response, guilt, then giving in
Pick one relationship and practice a Positive No there first
situations: A boss who sends last-minute requests
A roommate or relative who keeps borrowing things
Team requests that pile up unanswered
Recurring arguments that start with a small request

source.citation: William Ury, The Power of a Positive No (2007), introduction (the three-A trap); reader's guide question 3; PON note on Ury's NECN interview

insights.confidence_rationale: Credible expert framework confirmed in the publisher's reader's guide and Ury's own interview. It is a descriptive typology, not empirically tested; it resembles established conflict-style models (for example the accommodating and avoiding styles in Thomas-Kilmann), but that link is our observation, not the book's.

insights.name: Back Your No With a Plan B
insights.explanation: A no is much easier to say calmly when you already know what you will do if the other person does not accept it. Ury calls this your Plan B: your own best course of action that does not depend on their agreement (similar to the BATNA idea in Getting to Yes, applied to refusals). Once you have it, he suggests reassessing whether to say no at all by asking three questions: do I have a real interest at stake, do I have the power to back the no, and do I have the right to refuse here. If the other side pushes back, describe the consequences you will act on as a respectful warning about what you will do, not a threat meant to punish them.
insights.when_to_use: Before refusing someone who has power over you or who is likely to push back hard: a demanding client, a manager, a landlord, a family member who escalates.
insights.worked_example: A freelance designer wants to refuse a client's demand for unlimited free revisions. Before the call she works out her Plan B: if the client will not accept a revision limit, she will finish the current round, deliver the files, and end the engagement, which she can afford because another client wants her time. With that settled she can say, without heat, that the contract covers two rounds and additional rounds are billed hourly, and that if that does not work she will wrap up after this round. In a family, a woman deciding whether to refuse to host Thanksgiving again checks her interest (she is exhausted), her power (her siblings can host), and her right (no one is owed her labor) before saying no.
common_mistakes: Refusing with no plan for what happens if the other person says no to your no
Treating Plan B as a compromise you will accept, rather than an independent action you can take
Turning a statement of consequences into a threat
Skipping the check on whether you actually have the power or right to refuse
steps: Ask what you will do if the other person does not accept your no
Develop and, if needed, strengthen that independent option before the conversation
Reassess: do you have the interest, the power, and the right to say no here
Deliver your Positive No; keep Plan B in reserve rather than leading with it
If they push, state the consequence you will act on calmly, as information rather than punishment
situations: Turning down a manager's request when you expect pushback
Declining to host a family event
Saying no to a landlord's or vendor's demand

source.citation: William Ury, The Power of a Positive No (2007), Part I on preparing a Positive No (Plan B; chapter two's closing questions on interest, power and right); reader's guide questions 6, 7 and 11
source.underlying_research: Builds on the BATNA concept in Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes (1981); not separately tested for refusals.

insights.confidence_rationale: Plan B and the three questions are confirmed in the publisher's reader's guide; the underlying BATNA concept is a widely taught negotiation principle. The application to everyday refusals is expert practice rather than tested research.

supports_existing.note: Adds a concrete script for stating a limit while affirming the relationship: name what you are protecting, state the no plainly, then propose a specific alternative.

Ury's accommodate trap marks the limit of saying yes to every offer: accepting a request you should refuse harms both your interests and, through later resentment, the relationship. Accept the reality of the request, then answer it with a Positive No when needed.

still_unverified: The book text itself was not read; content comes from the publisher's reader's guide, PON pages, Ury's own site, and a blog summary citing p. 16.
Exact chapter placement of Plan B, the three questions, and the warning-versus-threat distinction is inferred from the reader's guide question order.
The chained pattern of the three traps (avoid, then attack, then accommodate) is from the Hyatt blog summary of the introduction, not confirmed in the book.

research_notes: The publisher's reader's guide was the richest legal source: it confirms Yes! No. Yes?, the three-A trap, going to the balcony, Plan B, the interest, power and right questions, attack words, warnings versus threats, and positions versus interests. Going to the balcony and positions versus interests were not extracted because they come from Ury's earlier books and likely overlap with the professional agent's Getting to Yes extraction; Plan B overlaps with BATNA and the orchestrator may wish to cross-reference it.
